analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans all oil, gas, and mineral drilling in the Arctic Ocean.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 39 House Democrats, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote in the Natural Resources Committee before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal law governing offshore energy to bar the Interior Department from issuing or renewing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort Sea and Chukchi Sea planning areas. Because the ban would be written into statute, no future administration could simply reverse it as a policy decision. It never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal and Alaska Native communities whose fisheries, hunting, and subsistence ways of life depend on a clean Arctic Ocean, the broader public through avoided climate and spill risks, and taxpayers who would not bear the costs of a remote offshore spill response.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal communities and the broader public

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Interior Department from issuing or renewing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort Sea and Chukchi Sea planning areas.
Writes the ban directly into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, so it would take an act of Congress to undo it rather than a change in administration policy.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies that hold or would seek leases in Arctic federal waters, and Alaska interests hoping for the jobs, production, and federal royalties that Arctic development could bring.

drawbacks.text: The prohibition covers not just oil and gas but every mineral, and applies to the Beaufort and Chukchi Sea planning areas, permanently removing a large federal offshore area from any development even if technology or safety practices improved later.

Blocking Arctic production means forgoing potential domestic energy supply, Alaska jobs, and federal royalty revenue; an honest supporter acknowledges the ban trades that economic value for environmental and climate protection rather than being cost-free.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is permanent protection of a fragile, hard-to-clean-up marine environment and a lock against future administrations reopening it, while its cost is forgone energy production and royalties from a region no company is currently producing from. The main design criticism is that the ban is written as an absolute statute covering all minerals, leaving no path to reopen the area if drilling technology changed; the main benefit is that the same permanence is what makes the protection credible.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced and to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee three weeks later, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Jared Huffman introduced the Stop Arctic Ocean Drilling Act of 2021 on January 28, 2021, with a list of original cosponsors.

The bill would prohibit the Interior Department from issuing or renewing any lease or authorization for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in the Arctic Ocean, including the Beaufort and Chukchi Sea planning areas.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on January 28, 2021, and to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on February 19, 2021.
No further action was taken for the remainder of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023, so the bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas companies and Alaska development interests are better off because the ban never became law, leaving the question of Arctic leasing open to future administrations instead of closed by statute.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drillers and Alaska development interests

for.name: Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote it to add a permanent Arctic Ocean leasing ban to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.

for.name: 38 of 222 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached the floor, so no vote ever tested the split.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar these companies from leasing or developing the Beaufort and Chukchi Sea planning areas of the Arctic Ocean. Their gain from the bill's failure is keeping that federal area open to future leasing, while the environmental and spill risks fall on coastal communities and the public.

Arctic offshore production is promoted as a source of Alaska jobs and federal royalties; the statutory ban would foreclose that economic path regardless of which party controlled the White House. The bill's death keeps that possibility alive.
